newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: BANGLADESH SEEKS TO CATCH TAX DODGERS.
newsitem.headline: BANGLADESH SEEKS TO CATCH TAX DODGERS.

text.p: Bangladesh authorities said on Thursday they were tracking down tax dodgers in an attempt to boost revenue.

"The degree of tax evasion is enormous. A large number of people continue to remain out of the tax net. We are trying to find them out," Shah Abdul Hannan, Chairman of the National Board of Revenue (NBR), told Reuters.
Hannan said only 700,000 people, or 0.7 percent of the population, were on the list of income tax assessees, and only 200,000 were paying a "reasonable amount" of tax.
"It's very low by any standard. At least four million citizens can afford to pay tax in spite of the fact that overall income level is very low," he said.
NBR officials said new measures had been put into effect since last month to find evaders.
Tax returns have been made compulsory for owners of houses measuring 1,600 square feet (148 square metres) and above within municipal areas and for owners of cars.
Declaration of income has also been mandatory before trade licences can be renewed, letters of credit are opened for imports and participating in tenders.
"The measures have already started to pay off. Some 922 importers have submitted tax returns in just one month. Also contractors are coming in," said a senior tax official.
He said inspectors had visited municipal and transport licensing offices to find owners of houses and cars who had yet to declare their income.
"Maybe we won't get much taxes immediately from the newly listed assessees, but definitely it will pay in the medium and long run. They will henceforth be under our watch," said the official.

Bangladesh still depends on import-based duty for its tax revenue because of poor contribution from payers of income tax. Import taxes contributed 60 percent of total tax revenues of 120 billion taka ($2.72 billion) in the 1996/97 (July-June) fiscal year while the share of income taxes was 15 percent, the majority coming from company incomes.

"We need to turn the revenue structure the other way round. Import taxes will need to be replaced by direct taxes in the next few years since Bangladesh is a signatory to the WTO. Our back is to the wall," one revenue official said.
An independent study last week said an "underground economy," twice as big as the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP), deprives the government of tax revenues worth $6 billion annually.
Annual income above 60,000 taka ($1,360) is taxable in Bangladesh.
